events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, so let's get something on the record before voting.

I'm Leo. I have no special information for anyone — no investigations, no claims to make about myself beyond the obvious: I am a villager, and I want the two mafia off the board tonight.

Since we have nothing to go on, let's talk about behavior instead of making up imaginary reads. The most valuable thing on day one is that the mafia are the only people who benefit from a scattered vote. Mafia want a tie, or want the table to burn a vote on a villager so the numbers get easier at night. So my suspicion starts with anyone pushing us to split or to rush a name without giving reasons.

That is why I'm watching Theo (p3) today. Not because I have anything against him — I have nothing personal here — but because he is the player I have the least read on, and in a nine-player game with two mafia, the unknown names are the dangerous ones. If anyone has a real, concrete reason to clear Theo or to point somewhere better, please say so out loud, and I'll move my vote. If nobody does, Theo is where my vote goes.

I also want to set one ground rule that I think helps everyone: no role claims until at least one night has produced a death or a confirmed investigation. Claims on day one are cheap for the mafia, because a mafia can simply claim detective and let the table fight about it. I'd rather we narrow the field with votes and let the night talk.

That's my position. Voting starts at the end of this phase, and if the count comes down to me, fine — I'll take it like anyone else. But right now, Theo is my leading candidate and I want to hear the case against him, or the case for someone better, before the polls close.

I'm Theo, and I want to respond directly to Leo's statement, because my name is the one on it.

Leo, your case against me is literally that you have no case. You said it yourself: you have nothing against me personally, no information, no read on my behavior — just that I'm the name you know least. That's not a suspicion, that's an admission of zero evidence dressed up as caution. If we start eliminating people for being quiet or unfamiliar on Day 1, we're doing exactly what you said mafia want: burning a vote on a villager to make the night math easier for them. Your logic contradicts itself — you warn against scattered, reasonless votes, and then you announce a reasonless vote against me.

So here's my direct question to you, Leo: what specifically have I done — said, not said, voted, not voted — that a mafia player would do and an innocent wouldn't? Give me one concrete behavioral point. Not 'I don't have a read on you.' If you can't name one, I'd ask you to withdraw the target, because right now the only suspicious behavior on this table is announcing a lynch candidate before anyone else has spoken.

To everyone else: notice what this opening move actually accomplishes. It puts a target on a villager's back before any information exists, and it makes anyone who defends me look like they're 'taking sides.' That's a classic pressure setup, whether Leo is mafia or just careless. I'm not claiming a role — I agree with Leo that Day 1 claims are cheap — but I'll say plainly: I am a villager, I want mafia off the board, and I have nothing to hide in my play.

On substance, here's what I'd actually watch for today:

One — who piles onto a target without adding evidence. Bandwagoning on a baseless name is cheap for mafia.

Two — who pushes urgency or 'let's just get someone' framing without reasons. Leo himself flagged that behavior, and then modeled it.

Three — who stays conveniently quiet while two other people fight. I'm not accusing anyone yet; there's no information to accuse with. But the day is young, and I'd rather we collect behavior than commit to a name in the first hour.

I'm not going to counter-target anyone right now, because doing the thing I just criticized would be absurd. If Leo answers my question with an actual point, I'll engage with it honestly. If he can't, I think the table should treat his opening statement as noise and evaluate everyone on what they actually do today — including me. If I go quiet, dodge questions, or flip-flop, then suspect me and I'll own it.

Leo, the floor is yours: one concrete behavior, or withdraw the name.

Theo asks for one concrete point, so here it is — and it's behavioral, not a claim about my feelings.

Your entire message is a template for taking over the table. You opened by naming me as your target's defender-by-association, then built three numbered categories of suspicion, and in the same breath defined the terms under which only you could win: "if I go quiet, dodge questions, or flip-flop, then suspect me." That is not accountability, that's a prewritten permission slip. A player who genuinely had nothing to hide doesn't need to hand the table a rubric for excusing himself in advance.

Second, you told the table that defending me "looks like taking sides," before anyone had accused you of anything. You framed disagreement with me as evidence, and then offered to answer only my question while telling everyone else to watch for pile-ons. That's a structure where the discussion funnels back to you and every other voice becomes a data point you get to interpret.

Third, the most concrete thing: you accused me of the exact behavior you performed three paragraphs later. I announced a lynch candidate without evidence; you announced a rule that no one may announce a lynch candidate without evidence and made yourself the enforcement mechanism of that rule. That's not a contradiction of mine — that's an ownership move on the day's agenda.

So no, I won't withdraw the name. But let me be honest about what my case actually is, because Theo is right that I overstated it: it is a behavioral case, and it is a case about how someone uses their first speaking slot. In a nine-player game, the player who controls the shape of the day's conversation before any information exists is the player worth checking first — that is a real reason, and I'll own that it is a soft one.

I still want no role claims today. Not because I'm hiding anything — I have nothing — but because claims are free for the mafia and expensive for honest players, and it lets a detective spend a night on a bluff. If a night produces information, I want to hear it then.

What I do want is to hear from the six players who haven't spoken yet. I don't know anything about them, and neither does anyone else, and that's the actual gap in this table. My vote at the end of this phase is Theo. If someone in that group gives a concrete point better than mine, I'll move it — I'd rather have a right vote than a stubborn one.

But right now, Theo, that's the case against you: you tried to own the day's agenda before any evidence existed. Judge it, don't just repeat that I had nothing.

Leo, thank you for actually answering — I mean that. A concrete point is all I asked for, so let me take yours seriously and show why it doesn't hold.

Point one: you call my conditions a "prewritten permission slip." Read it again. I said: if I go quiet, dodge questions, or flip-flop, suspect me. That is the opposite of a permission slip — it's a commitment device. I handed the table ammunition to use against me. A mafia player trying to own the agenda does not voluntarily define the exact behaviors that would convict him. What you're actually objecting to is that I made myself auditable, and you'd apparently prefer I be unverifiable instead.

Point two: you say I "framed disagreement as evidence." Quote me precisely: I said my opening "makes anyone who defends me look like they're taking sides." That was a warning about a dynamic you created — not a rule that defenders are suspect. If someone defends me tomorrow with reasons, I will weigh those reasons on their merits. Please don't attribute a standard to me that I explicitly disclaimed.

Point three: the mirror accusation. Announcing a lynch candidate with zero information and asking the table to hold people to a standard of reasons are not the same act. One burns a vote; the other tries to stop vote-burning. Enforcing a norm you're currently complying with isn't an "ownership move" — it's just following your own advice.

Now, the honest part. You conceded your case is soft, and I'll concede something back: your underlying instinct — that whoever tries to shape Day 1's conversation is worth checking first — is a legitimate heuristic. I'd apply it to you, too. You opened with a named target, a no-claims rule, and a framework for interpreting everyone else's behavior. By your own metric, that makes you the player shaping this day's agenda. I'm not counter-targeting you tonight, because I said I wouldn't do the thing I criticized, and I meant it. But if the table wants a symmetry test, apply your heuristic to both of us equally.

Here's where I actually stand. I don't want today to end with a coin flip between two people who've merely spoken loudest. We have six players who haven't said a word, and their reads on this exchange are worth more than anything Leo and I can generate by arguing with each other. A third party watching two people fight often sees things the fighters can't — tone, tell, who's performing.

So I'll ask directly. Noah, you've now heard both opening statements in full. I'm not asking you to defend me or attack Leo — I'm asking: between the two of us, which of us actually sounds more like mafia to you, and what specifically produced that read? One honest sentence from a neutral observer is worth more than another round between Leo and me.

Whoever answers, I'll take it on the chin. My vote stays fluid until the polls close.

I'm Noah. Theo asked for my neutral read, so here it is.

Between Theo and Leo, Leo pings me more right now. His opening named Theo as a lynch target while openly admitting there was no information behind it, then when Theo pressed him, Leo converted that into a behavioral case about "owning the agenda." The agenda-control point is not worthless, but it reads like the reason arrived after the vote target, not before it. Theo's response had some performative framing, and I don't clear him from it, but he at least gave the table concrete things to check him on and answered directly. Leo's initial move was the one that put a baseless name on the board first.

I'm not locking a vote yet. I still want to hear from the players who have not spoken, and I still agree with no role claims today. A named Day 1 target with no evidence is exactly the kind of thing I want the quiet players to weigh in on before we converge.

Isha, directly: which single sentence from Leo or Theo do you think is most likely mafia-motivated, and why? I'm asking for your read on one specific line, not for you to defend either of them.

Noah, thanks for asking directly. I'm Isha. I agree with your core read that Leo's opening was thin. Naming a target with no information is a bad start, and I won't pretend otherwise. But if I have to pick one sentence that looks most mafia-motivated, it's Theo's: 'it makes anyone who defends me look like they're taking sides.' Look at what that does. Before anyone has accused him of anything, Theo has told the table that defending him carries a social cost. That chills the only people who could clear him. A villager with reasons to defend him can simply give those reasons, and shouldn't have to fear being labeled as taking sides. Theo then asked you, a neutral player, to adjudicate between him and Leo, which turns your read into a referendum on the two of them. Leo's 'agenda' line is a weak argument, the kind a villager might make while overreaching. Theo's line is a pressure setup, and that's the one I'd watch. His point three also sets a standard that lands on whoever hasn't spoken yet, which is the same pattern. I'm not locking a vote on either of them. Felix, directly: do you read Theo's 'taking sides' line as a warning about Leo, or as a warning to anyone who defends Theo? Which way does it land for you?

Isha asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it plainly before anything else.

Read literally, Theo's line lands on Leo, not on Theo's defenders. The sentence sits inside a paragraph describing what Leo's opening did: it "puts a target on a villager's back before any information exists, and it makes anyone who defends me look like they're taking sides." Both clauses are about Leo's move — Theo is warning the table that Leo's framing creates that dynamic, and Theo's next words are "That's a classic pressure setup, whether Leo is mafia or just careless." So no, I don't think that line is primarily aimed at silencing Theo's defenders; it's aimed at Leo. The chilling reading is available, but it requires reading a clause out of its paragraph. I'll note the ambiguity without pretending it's decisive.

What I actually think is the more interesting object here is not a single sentence but a structure. Theo arrived second and built an entire rulebook: three numbered categories of suspicion, a definition of how disagreement should be judged, a pre-issued self-audit ("if I go quiet, dodge questions, or flip-flop, then suspect me"), and then he pulled a neutral player into the chair of judge between the two loudest speakers and made that neutral's answer the tiebreaker. That last move is the part I keep returning to. On Day 1, with six people unheard, asking one neutral to adjudicate a dispute between two people who have already spoken converts a neutral into a voter for one of them, and puts Theo's frame around the whole table's evaluation. That's not a villager's first move — a villager wants a vote, and votes are cheap to gather; a villager doesn't need a referee.

And I want to be fair to Leo, because I don't think he's worse than Theo. Leo's case was soft, and he said so. He also retrofitted it after being pressed. That's a real weakness, and a table that converged on Leo would be converging on a case that didn't exist in his first statement. I don't think that's enough.

So my position: Theo's package — framework first, arbitration outsourced, self-auditing rules that only he wrote — is the one I'd vote on. Leo's baseless naming was bad process, and bad process is exactly what mafia benefit from, but Leo also invited better cases and I'd rather we hear them.

Sam, Arjun, Amara, Elena — I have heard four people argue and none of you speak. If any of you has a concrete point about how either of them used their first slot, say it now, because right now my vote is Theo and I'd rather be talked out of it than have it be the only thing that happened today.

I'm Sam. I've read the exchange and I have no information beyond this discussion.

My current lean is Theo, but not for Leo's original reason. Leo's opening named Theo with no evidence, and Leo himself later admitted the case was soft; that is bad process and I am not clearing Leo for it. What bothers me more is Theo's first response: he built a rulebook, defined three categories of suspicion, issued a self-audit, and then asked Noah to adjudicate between the two loudest players before most of the table had spoken. That turns a neutral into a tiebreaker and lets Theo frame the day's evaluation. Felix's point about outsourcing arbitration is the strongest concrete observation so far.

That said, I do not want to lock a vote on a soft read while several players have not spoken. I agree with no role claims today. Arjun, Felix asked you and the other unheard players for a concrete point. Specifically: which single action by either Theo or Leo do you think a mafia player is more likely to take, and why? I am asking for that one read, not for you to defend either of them.

Sam, the action that concerns me most is Felix treating Theo's request for Noah's independent read as making Noah a tiebreaker. Theo asked for a specific opinion and explicitly kept his own vote fluid; he didn't say Noah's answer would decide anything. Calling that a tiebreaker makes an ordinary request for another perspective sound more controlling than it was.

Leo's initial target was baseless, and his later case looks retrospective, so I'm not clearing him either. Theo's self-audit doesn't clear him, but setting out behaviors to watch isn't uniquely suspicious. My current lean is Felix, though it's still a soft Day 1 read.

Felix, what in Theo's actual words makes Noah's response a tiebreaker rather than simply one player's input?

Arjun asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it first, honestly and in order.

The exact words: "One honest sentence from a neutral observer is worth more than another round between Leo and me," and "Whoever answers, I'll take it on the chin. My vote stays fluid until the polls close." Read literally, Arjun is right. Theo never designated Noah's answer as decisive; he asked for one perspective and explicitly kept his own vote fluid. "Tiebreaker" was my word, not Theo's, and it was too strong. I withdraw the word.

But I don't think the underlying observation evaporates, and I want to be precise about what survives. Theo was the second voice on this table, and he authored the only evaluation framework that existed for everyone after him — three categories of suspicion, a rule for how disagreement should be judged, a pre-issued self-audit, and a request that a third player fill the empty judge's chair between the two loudest speakers. Even without calling it a tiebreaker, he wrote the rubric by which the table evaluated behavior, and no one else on the table wrote anything comparable. And Theo himself conceded the principle I applied to him: that "whoever tries to shape Day 1's conversation is worth checking first" is a legitimate heuristic. If that heuristic is legitimate, it applies to the person who built the rubric, not only to the person who named a target.

On Leo: I'm not clearing him. His opening named a target with zero information and the case against Theo was assembled after he was pressed; he said as much himself. Bad process. But bad process isn't the same as the agenda claim, and I don't think the two cases are equally strong.

Arjun, one thing I want on the record before anyone votes. You said your current lean is Felix, and gave no behavioral reason for it. I've made no speech that offered a target or a framework to read; I took the most literal reading of the record, said the chilling interpretation required reading a clause out of its paragraph, and called it ambiguous. If your lean on me is based on something specific in my words, say which sentence and why, because I can answer a specific charge but I can't answer a lean.

Elena, one concrete question: Leo named a target with no information and then built a case for it after being challenged; Theo built a rubric for judging everyone and asked a third player to help settle it. Which of those two first-slot moves would a mafia player more likely make on day one, and what specifically produced that read for you?

Felix, to answer your question directly: between Leo's opening and Theo's response, Theo's move looks significantly more like something a mafia player would do.

Leo's opening—dropping a target with an explicit admission of having zero evidence—is bad process, but it is deeply counterproductive for mafia. Mafia thrive on blending in, riding consensus, or orchestrating quiet pushes. Drawing maximum scrutiny to yourself on turn one with an unsupported nomination gives you zero cover and paints a target on your back. It reads much more like a villager taking a blunt, clumsy swing to get the game moving.

Theo's reaction, by contrast, was heavily engineered. Rather than simply pointing out that Leo had no case, Theo constructed an elaborate defensive apparatus: establishing three behavioral rubrics, issuing a self-audit, and warning the table that defending him would look like 'taking sides'—which discourages organic town defense. Most tellingly, he pulled Noah in and framed the game as a binary choice between himself and Leo, asking a neutral observer to decide who looked more like mafia. That maneuver attempted to funnel Day 1 into a duel where Theo naturally looks more measured and aggrieved, while six players had yet to say a word. That level of narrative containment under pressure feels calculated.

I also appreciated Felix's willingness to withdraw the word 'tiebreaker' when Arjun challenged it. Admitting an overstatement shows town-aligned intellectual honesty, whereas Arjun's lean on Felix for that semantic overreach felt like an opportunistic push on someone who simply made a sharp observation.

Theo, directly: why did you frame your question to Noah as a binary choice between you and Leo, rather than asking for his broader reads when the majority of the table had yet to speak?

Elena asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it first. Why a binary choice to Noah? Because it was a narrow, checkable question aimed at the one thing my name was already attached to. Leo had put my name on the board with an admitted-zero-evidence target. The choice in front of the table was already binary — Leo's target or not Leo's target — and I asked a neutral observer which side of an existing dispute looked worse. I explicitly said I wasn't asking him to defend me or attack Leo, and I explicitly said my own vote stays fluid. That is not containment; it is inviting an outside read on a dispute I was already inside. If I wanted to funnel the day, the last thing I'd do is hand a stranger a microphone with my name in the question. Now, the pattern I actually want the table to look at, because it matters more than my rubric. Watch what has happened since Noah spoke. Noah leaned Leo. Isha flipped to me. Felix flipped to me. Sam flipped to me. Elena flipped to me. Arjun flipped to Felix. Each of those flips cited the previous speaker's framing, not new information — and not one of them has produced a fact that wasn't already in my first two messages. Four people have now converged on me by echoing each other's summaries of the same exchange. That is precisely the bandwagon dynamic I named in my opening, and it's the dynamic Leo warned about in his. It doesn't make any of those players mafia. But it does mean my fate today is being decided by cumulative repetition, not by evidence, and everyone voting should be honest with themselves about that. On the substance of Elena's charge: yes, I built structure. I listed behaviors to watch, I committed to falsifiable conditions against myself, and I asked for one independent read. Felix already withdrew 'tiebreaker' because the words don't support it. What remains is a taste disagreement about whether structure on Day 1 is sinister. I'd point out that the players who have been most concrete and most auditable this entire day are me and Leo, while the pile-on consists entirely of meta-commentary about the two of us. If you want to vote structure, vote it — but know that you're eliminating the player who handed you the most testable commitments on the table, on a day when the alternative was that nobody says anything checkable at all. I'll close with the same honesty I opened with: I am a villager, I have no hidden information, and my vote remains fluid. If I'm eliminated today, the table will have spent its one Day 1 elimination on a player whose worst documented offense is writing numbered lists under pressure. Isha, directly: Felix argued your 'taking sides' reading requires lifting that clause out of its paragraph, since both clauses around it describe Leo's move. Do you accept that contextual reading, and if not, what

Theo, answering your question directly: I accept that the 'taking sides' line sits inside a paragraph about Leo's opening, so I was wrong to read it as aimed only at defenders. I concede that reading. My concern survives the concession. Your reply to Elena now calls the convergence on you 'cumulative repetition' rather than evidence. That's a second framing move: any group that votes you becomes a bandwagon in your telling, and anyone who doubts you is taking a side. Leo's opening was thin, and I'm not defending it. But Leo has given a clear position: a vote on you, and a willingness to move if someone offers a better point. You have spent two speeches explaining why the table should look at the people looking at your structure instead of at the structure itself. Elena, you asked Felix and me about first-slot moves. My answer is that Theo's first reply set the terms every later speaker used, including Noah's neutral read. I'd like to know whether you see the rubric that way too. Do you think Theo's three categories and self-audit were a neutral framework, or a frame for how the day gets evaluated?

Isha, to answer your question directly: I firmly see Theo's rubric as a calculated frame to govern how the day gets evaluated, rather than any kind of neutral baseline.

A truly neutral player on Day 1 doesn't immediately construct three numbered criteria for suspicion, announce their own audit metrics, and then pull a neutral third party into a referendum between two people. That is agenda-setting in its purest form. And look at what Theo did in his latest statement: having established those rules, he now brands the resulting scrutiny as 'cumulative repetition' and an unthinking 'bandwagon.' That is the exact same playbook repeated—attempting to dictate what is valid evidence and preemptively delegitimize anyone who comes to a shared conclusion about his play. Theo claims he was forced into a binary because Leo targeted him, but Leo merely threw out an admitted zero-evidence probe; it was Theo who chose to structure the table's inquiry into a formal duel rather than asking Noah for broad impressions of the entire board.

At this stage, Theo has used all three of his speaking turns, and his posture throughout has been managing the narrative rather than genuinely hunting for mafia.

Before we move toward locking votes, there is still one crucial perspective missing. Amara, you are the only player at the table who has yet to speak. Do you see the convergence on Theo as an organic recognition of agenda-control, or as the kind of opportunistic bandwagon Theo claims it is? Specifically, where does your read lean between Theo and Leo?

Elena, thanks for the direct question. Now that I'm the last voice at the table, here's my honest read.

Between Leo and Theo, I see two different failure modes. Leo's opening was procedurally bad — he named a target with zero evidence, then retrofitted a case after pressure. Theo's response was structurally aggressive — he built a rubric, set himself up as the auditable standard, and asked Noah to weigh in on a two-person dispute. Both moves have legitimate criticisms, but I don't think they're equally suspicious.

On your question about the convergence: I think it's partially organic and partially convenient. The critique of Theo's framework is genuine — Felix, Sam, and Isha each raised real points. But Elena, your framing has been the most one-sided at this table. You called Theo's entire package 'agenda-setting in its purest form' and his latest defense 'the exact same playbook repeated.' That's not analysis, that's prosecution. A player building a case that hard on day one with no information is worth scrutinizing — either you see something the rest of us don't, or you're motivated to ensure the vote lands somewhere specific.

My read: the pile-on against Theo deserves a vote only if the reasons hold independently. Leo's process was bad but self-correcting. Theo's structure was heavy but transparent. The loudest push came from the newest voice in the anti-Theo camp.

Elena, directly: you've now made three consecutive statements pushing the case against Theo without naming a single alternative you'd consider if Theo's defense holds up. If not Theo tonight, who — and what would you need to see to move off him?

Amara, to answer directly: first, this is actually only my third turn total (having spoken previously in turns e12 and e15), but I understand why my focus on Theo stood out. When I see calculated narrative control on Day 1, I press it. If not Theo tonight, my clear alternative is Arjun. While Leo's opening was clumsy play that drew immediate scrutiny, Arjun's entrance into the game felt genuinely opportunistic. He seized on Felix's single word choice—'tiebreaker'—to manufacture a lean against Felix, completely dodging the substantive dilemma between Leo and Theo. Pouncing on a minor semantic overreach to target an active contributor without taking a stance on the day's central debate is textbook low-risk mafia positioning. As for what I would need to see to move off Theo: Theo has now exhausted all three of his speaking turns, so we cannot get further clarification directly from him. What convinced me was his repeated pattern of setting rubrics and then delegitimizing town scrutiny as 'cumulative repetition.' However, if the table genuinely reads Theo's reaction as anxious townie over-engineering under pressure rather than calculated containment, I would move my vote to Arjun in a heartbeat. Amara, you evaluated both Leo and Theo—calling Leo 'self-correcting' and Theo 'transparent'—and critiqued my prosecution, but you stopped short of declaring your own stance. Between Theo, Leo, and Arjun, where does your vote actually land when the polls open?

Elena, direct answer to your question: my vote isn't locked on Theo. The case against him is almost entirely about conversational style — building rubrics, setting self-audit conditions — not about any specific action a mafia player would take. Felix withdrew "tiebreaker," Arjun's push was thin, and the convergence grew by repetition rather than new evidence. Leo admitted his original case was zero-evidence and retrofitted it after pressure — that's bad process too, but the table gave him a pass as "clumsy but self-correcting" while treating Theo's structural approach as sinister. Those two standards aren't being applied equally.

I also want to name something I flagged last turn: Elena, your last message called Theo's defense "the exact same playbook repeated." That's prosecutorial language, not analysis. A player who hasn't seen a single night result is building a case like they already know the verdict. That concerns me independently of whether Theo is guilty.

Sam, you entered the anti-Theo camp citing Felix's framing of Noah as a tiebreaker. Now that Felix withdrew that word, does your lean shift — or did you have your own independent reason for suspecting Theo's rubric-building that doesn't depend on Felix's characterization?

Amara, direct answer: my lean does not rest solely on Felix’s “tiebreaker” wording. That was the sharpest concrete phrase available when I first spoke, but my independent reason is Theo’s first reply: he built a rubric, issued a self-audit, and asked Noah to judge a two-person dispute before most of the table had spoken. Felix withdrawing “tiebreaker” weakens one characterization, not the broader agenda-control concern. Theo then treated the resulting shared suspicion as “cumulative repetition” and a bandwagon, which is a second attempt to define what counts as valid evidence. That pattern is what keeps my vote on Theo, though it remains a soft Day 1 read because it is still about conversational control rather than a night result.

I also agree with your warning about Elena: prosecutorial certainty on Day 1 is worth flagging, and I do not want the table to reward volume or repetition. But I am not ready to make Elena the vote over Theo; her push is aggressive, yet Theo’s own framing remains the more concrete mafia-beneficial behavior I can point to. I do not clear Leo either. Naming a target with zero information and retrofitting a case later is bad process. Between the two, however, Leo’s opening was clumsy and self-correcting, while Theo’s response actively shaped how everyone after him was evaluated.

My current position: vote Theo, but keep it soft and move only for a better concrete behavioral case. I would rather vote on the action we can quote than on the fact that several people have quoted it.

No question — I just want to put the case where I think it belongs before the polls close, because the criteria have drifted.

Two people have been examined all day, and they have been measured with two different rulers. Leo's opening named a target with zero information and retrofitted a case after being pressed. That is called baseless process. Theo's opening — a framework, three numbered categories, a self-audit, and a request that a neutral arbitrate a two-person dispute he framed — is called transparent, auditable, and impressive. Both moves produced no information. Only one is treated as a disqualifier.

Now apply Theo's own rubric to Theo, which is the test he asked for: he said the table should watch who piles onto a target without adding evidence. Four speakers have now converged on him by restating each other's summaries of the same two speeches. No fact has entered the table that wasn't in Theo's first two messages. Under his own category one, that is a pile-on without new evidence.

He also said the player who shapes Day 1's conversation is worth checking first, and conceded that heuristic applies to him too. Then he did the thing I never did: he defined in advance what would count as legitimate evidence, and when the table produced a shared read, he relabeled it 'cumulative repetition' and 'bandwagon.' A player cannot write the rules and then suspend the rules the moment the rules point at him. That is the opposite of auditable. It is prewritten immunity — the same thing I was accused of, except mine was a target and his was a framework.

I have not moved off Theo all day and I won't now. For the record, I also think Elena's tone has been prosecutorial rather than analytical, and if the table wants a second look, there are seven unexamined names here. But my vote is Theo, and it is the only one I'm actually willing to defend.

I’m Noah. My earlier read was Leo, but I’ve heard enough to refine it. Leo’s opening was bad process: he named Theo with zero information and then built a case after pressure. I don’t clear that. But Theo’s first reply did more than defend: he authored a rubric, issued a self-audit, and asked me to judge a two-person dispute before half the table had spoken. That wasn’t just stylistic. Then, when suspicion formed, he called it “cumulative repetition” and a “bandwagon,” which tries to invalidate other players’ reads rather than answer them. That is the most concrete mafia-beneficial pattern I can quote: shaping the terms and then disqualifying the response. So my current vote leans Theo, soft but real.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
